name: Facial exerciser
lead: Facial exercisers are small silicone or resistance devices held in the mouth or against the cheeks to work the smile, cheek and jaw muscles. People use them alongside facial yoga routines to aim for fuller cheeks, a firmer-looking lower face and a more defined or youthful appearance. The underlying idea is that repeated contraction against resistance may strengthen or enlarge facial muscles, as strength training does elsewhere in the body, so that the face looks fuller and more toned.

No published trial has tested a commercial facial exerciser device for appearance. Research on facial exercise as a technique is limited: a 2014 systematic review found that all nine included studies reported positive outcomes but none used a control group or randomization, and concluded that the evidence was insufficient to judge effectiveness.[1] A 2018 single-arm study of a 20-week facial exercise program in middle-aged women reported modest improvement in cheek fullness and estimated age.[2] A 2024 case report of a jaw exerciser found no change in two users.[3]
Facial exercise is also an established part of rehabilitation for facial palsy, which is a separate use.

paras: Devices include mouth-held silicone trainers that the user bites or presses with the lips, resistance bands for the cheeks, and jaw exercisers. They are usually accompanied by routines of repeated holds or reps, much like facial yoga.

Facial exercise as a practice is broader than the devices. Wikipedia's article on facial toning separates active methods, which use repeated voluntary contractions of specific muscle groups, from passive methods, which use electrostimulation through electrodes and conductive gel, and notes that proponents believe strengthening the muscles can tighten and plump the skin.[9] Resistance trainers are sold as a way to add load to the same idea, in the way a weight adds load to a limb.

The claimed mechanism is that resisted contraction increases the size or tone of facial muscles, so that the face looks fuller or firmer. The 2018 study authors measured outcomes with photographic aging scales rather than direct muscle measurements.[2] Whether this changes appearance meaningfully has not been established, and the authors of the jaw-exerciser case report argued that the chewing muscles targeted by such devices do not directly affect submental fat, jaw structure or skin elasticity.[3] Related passive devices instead use electrical stimulation to make facial muscles contract [9]. The 2018 research letter, indexed in PubMed as 'Association of Facial Exercise With the Appearance of Aging', is the main published exercise-and-appearance study [10].

Skeletal muscle elsewhere in the body enlarges when it is loaded repeatedly, and facial muscles are skeletal muscles that attach to skin. This is the basis of the proposed chain: loaded contraction, muscle growth, added volume under the skin, fuller cheeks and a firmer contour. In announcing their 2018 study, the Northwestern investigators said that in their view the exercises "enlarge and strengthen the facial muscles," and senior author Emily Poon said muscle growth was increasing facial volume. The study itself did not image muscle, so this mechanism is the authors' interpretation.[11][2]

Facial exercise sits between two older traditions: rehabilitation programmes that retrain facial movement after nerve injury, and cosmetic routines marketed as a non-surgical lift. Wikipedia's article on facial toning describes it both as a cosmetic procedure aimed at tone and volume and as a physical-therapy tool for stroke survivors and people with facial paralysis such as Bell's palsy.[9]

The most widely cited appearance study came out of Northwestern University's dermatology department and appeared in JAMA Dermatology on 3 January 2018. The exercise regimen came from Gary Sikorski of Happy Face Yoga, who co-authored the paper; lead author Murad Alam and senior author Emily Poon described it in the university announcement as the first scientific study to test facial exercise for appearance.[11][2] Alam said in the announcement that the participants' estimated age fell by almost three years over 20 weeks.[11] Coverage of face yoga in mainstream media has since been both enthusiastic and sceptical; a first-person Guardian essay on the practice drew discussion on Lemmy.[8]

Mouth-held silicone trainers and jaw exercisers extend the same idea to a physical object that adds resistance. Their discussion in looksmaxxing spaces tends to sit beside jaw and cheek training and mewing, rather than beside rehabilitation.[9]
No studies found of commercial facial exercise devices for appearance outcomes. Related research on facial exercise as a technique follows.

A 2014 systematic review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal identified nine reports of facial exercises for facial rejuvenation. All reported positive outcomes, but they were case reports, small case series or single-group before-and-after studies, and most assessments were subjective and unblinded. The authors concluded that the evidence was insufficient to determine effectiveness and that large randomized trials were needed.[1]

In a 2018 research letter in JAMA Dermatology, 27 adults aged 40 to 65 enrolled in a 20-week single-arm study of a 32-exercise program, and 16 women completed it. Blinded raters scored upper cheek fullness from 1.8 to 1.1 and lower cheek fullness from 1.6 to 0.9 on photoscales, and estimated mean age fell from 50.8 to 48.1 years; other measures did not change significantly. Limitations included the small sample, high dropout, no control group and lack of blinding of participants and administrators. One author founded the company whose regimen was used, and the study was funded by departmental funds.[2]

The 2018 study was reported by Northwestern as the first scientific test of whether facial exercise improves appearance. It enrolled 27 women aged 40 to 65, of whom 16 completed the programme; participants received two 90-minute in-person training sessions, then did 32 exercises for 30 minutes daily for eight weeks and every other day through week 20. Dermatologist raters judging standardised photographs found improvement in upper and lower cheek fullness, and estimated average age fell from 50.8 to 48.1 years. The authors listed the small, all-female, middle-aged sample and the lack of a control group as limitations and called for confirmation in a larger study.[11][10]

A 2024 case report of two men who used a commercially available jaw exerciser for about three months found no change in double chin, jawline or neck tightness in photographs, with no objective measurements. Both participants were also authors.[3]

Systematic reviews and Cochrane reviews have examined facial exercise and physical therapy for facial palsy (Bell's palsy).[4][5] Randomized trials have also studied post-injection facial exercise with botulinum toxin and face yoga in temporomandibular dysfunction.[6][7] These address function or treatment response rather than cosmetic rejuvenation. A 2011 meta-analysis and a 2022 updated systematic review looked at facial exercise therapy for facial palsy, and the 2022 review was also written to inform telerehabilitation.[12][4]

No safety studies of commercial facial exercisers have been published. Commonly reported issues are muscle soreness, jaw tension and gagging with intraoral devices; users in the jaw-exerciser case report reported dissatisfaction with gagging and suction.[3]

Wikipedia's article on facial toning places facial exercise within cosmetic and rehabilitative practice: active routines use repeated voluntary contractions, while passive versions use electrostimulation, with electrodes and conductive gel on points of the face to trigger muscle contractions. It calls the scientific support preliminary, citing the 2018 Alam study as having no control group [9]. Its descriptions of the aims of such routines (tightening and plumping the outer skin through muscle, skin and lymphatic stimulation) are tagged there as needing citation [9].

Facial exercise devices are discussed with jaw and cheek training routines as non-invasive ways to improve facial contour, often next to mewing, chewing gum and jaw trainers. The only controlled-style evidence is the small 2018 study of an exercise program rather than a device.

Mainstream media has also covered face yoga. A Guardian first-person piece headlined with a writer's regret at the time spent on it was shared and discussed on Lemmy, with a standfirst noting that famous, beautiful people love face yoga and asking whether it does anything [8].

lore.intro: Facial exercise and face yoga circulate in beauty media and on forums as a no-needle route to a more sculpted face; mouth-held trainers are an extension of the same idea [8].

claims.claim: Face exercises build cheek volume the way lifting builds muscle
claims.believers: Proponents argue facial muscles respond to resistance training, so trainers add volume under the cheeks and lift the lower face.
claims.experts: A 2018 single-arm study of a 20-week program reported modest gains in cheek fullness on photoscales, with no control group, high dropout and a founder-author conflict [2]; a 2014 systematic review found the evidence insufficient to judge effectiveness [1].

claims.claim: Jaw exercisers define the jawline and reduce a double chin
claims.believers: Users report using jaw exercisers in the hope of sharper jaw and neck lines.
claims.experts: A 2024 case report of two men found no photographic change in double chin, jawline or neck after about three months, and noted the chewing muscles targeted do not act directly on submental fat [3].

claims.claim: Facial exercise works because it is already used in rehabilitation
claims.believers: Supporters point to physiotherapy for facial palsy as proof that facial muscles can be trained.
claims.experts: Reviews of facial exercise therapy for Bell's palsy address functional recovery, not cosmetic outcomes [4][5].

claims.claim: Facial exercise can take years off your face
claims.believers: The Northwestern investigators said participants' apparent age fell by almost three years over 20 weeks [11].
claims.experts: The estimated age change came from rater scoring of photographs in 16 completers with no control group, and the authors called for a larger confirmation study [11][2].

claims.claim: Face yoga is simply passive electrical stimulation without the device
claims.believers: Some routines describe voluntary contractions as the free version of electrode-based facial toning.
claims.experts: Wikipedia distinguishes active exercise from passive electrostimulation, and notes that claims about plumping the skin and lymphatic stimulation lack citations [9].

angle.text: Users do timed holds or repetitions with a mouth-held silicone trainer or cheek band, hoping to build tone or volume in the cheek and smile muscles. The only controlled-style data come from a facial exercise program rather than a device, where blinded raters scored upper and lower cheek fullness as improved [2].
